summaries.example: Imagine a white ball and a white cup. They are different objects, but they share whiteness. A metaphysician might ask: Is whiteness a real feature shared by both things, or is “white” only a word we use for them? Another question is whether the ball stays the same object when it is painted blue. These questions go beyond simply describing what we see; they ask what reality is made of and how things remain the same.
summaries.summary: Metaphysics is the part of philosophy that asks broad questions about reality. Long ago, it was often connected with being itself, the first causes of things, and things that do not change. Today, its questions are wider. Philosophers ask what kinds of things exist, whether qualities such as whiteness are real, what makes something a substance, and how objects stay the same through change. They also study possibility, space and time, causes, free will, the mind and body, and social things such as groups and institutions. There is no single agreed definition or method. Some philosophers connect metaphysics closely with science; others study what is most basic or what depends on what. Some even argue that metaphysics is impossible, either because its questions lack meaning or because people cannot reliably answer them.
key_ideas: Metaphysics is difficult to define because its topics have changed over time.
Earlier metaphysics focused on being, first causes, unchanging things, categories, universals, and substances.
Modern metaphysics also asks about possibility, time, objects, causes, freedom, the mind, the physical world, and social life.
Philosophers disagree about whether metaphysical questions can be answered and what methods should be used.
summaries.why_it_matters: Metaphysics helps us notice assumptions hidden in ordinary ideas. When we ask whether a changing object is still the same, whether choices can be free, or whether a group is more than its members, we are asking metaphysical questions. Thinking carefully about them can make our ideas clearer, even when philosophers do not agree on one answer.

important_terms.definition: The study of very general questions about what exists, what things are like, and how reality is put together.
Being real or existing. Metaphysicians may ask what it means for anything to be at all.
A feature or quality that can belong to many things, such as whiteness or being round.
Something thought to exist in its own right, rather than only as a feature of another thing.
A way something could be, even if it is not the way things actually are.

questions_to_think_about: What makes something the same object after it changes?
Is whiteness something real, or only a word we use?
Could a person have acted differently if the past and laws of nature fixed only one future?
How might a team, a school, or money exist as a social thing?

summaries.example: Consider a gold statue. The gold may have existed before the statue was shaped, and it could survive being melted, while the statue could not survive that change. This raises a material-constitution problem: are the statue and the lump of gold one object or two objects in the same place? One proposal says constitution is a relation beyond ordinary part-whole relations. Other proposals try to explain the case through identity and parthood alone. The example shows how metaphysics can challenge everyday assumptions about objects and identity.
summaries.summary: Metaphysics is hard to delimit because its subject matter has expanded from the concerns associated with Aristotle’s first philosophy. Traditional topics include being as such, first causes, unchanging things, categories of being, universals, and substance. Contemporary metaphysics adds questions about modality, space and time, persistence, material constitution, causation, free will, the relation between mental and physical states, and socially constructed entities and categories. The debates are not limited to asking what exists. They also ask what makes one fact or entity depend on another, which features are fundamental, and whether a proposed theory explains reality well. For example, theories of modality use possible worlds in different ways, while theories of universals disagree about whether properties exist independently, only in their instances, or not at all. The entry also presents skeptical views: metaphysics may lack internal unity, may make meaningless claims, or may ask meaningful questions that human beings cannot answer reliably.
key_ideas: The historical subject of metaphysics was often described as being as such, first causes, or unchanging things, but contemporary usage is broader.
The problem of universals concerns whether shared properties and relations are real and how they relate to particular objects; realism and nominalism offer opposing approaches.
Substance theories ask which things exist in their own right and how they retain determinate identities through time and possible circumstances.
Contemporary debates include modality, space and time, persistence and constitution, causation, freedom and determinism, the mental and physical, and social metaphysics.
Methodological proposals appeal variously to science, ontological commitment, fundamental structure, or grounding and explanatory relations.
Challenges to metaphysics range from claims that its statements are meaningless to claims that they are meaningful but beyond reliable human knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Metaphysical assumptions influence how we understand persons, objects, science, time, responsibility, and social institutions. The field also tests the limits of philosophical explanation. Studying its disagreements teaches us to distinguish questions about existence from questions about dependence, meaning, explanation, and evidence, rather than treating every disagreement as if it were the same kind of problem.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical investigation of reality at the most general level, including existence, kinds of things, dependence, and what is fundamental.
The question of what it is for something to exist or to be, sometimes studied as being considered in general.
A property or relation that can be instantiated by multiple particular things, such as whiteness or being north of something.
A purported basic entity that exists in its own right and can serve as a subject of properties rather than existing in another thing.
Modality concerning what could or could not be true of a proposition; modality concerning what could or could not be true of a thing is called de re modality.
A complete possible way reality might be, used by some philosophers to analyze necessity and possibility.
The relation by which one thing or fact is said to depend on, explain, or be made more basic by another.
The view that universals exist or have being; nominalism denies that universals exist in that way.

questions_to_think_about: Does a theory need to posit universals to explain why two objects are both white?
If determinism leaves only one physically possible future, can an agent still be free? If indeterminism leaves several futures, does chance help?
Are possible worlds abstract states of affairs, or could they be concrete universes distinct from ours?
Should facts about tables be grounded in facts about their parts, or should the table be more fundamental?
What would count as a good method for deciding a metaphysical dispute?

summaries.example: Suppose a sculptor shapes a lump of clay into a statue. The clay can survive being flattened, but the statue cannot survive that change and still be the same statue. Are there two things in one place—the clay and the statue—or just one thing described in two ways? Philosophers use puzzles like this to ask what makes objects the same, whether objects can share a location, and whether “constitution” is different from simply being made of parts.
summaries.summary: Metaphysics asks what reality is like at a very general level. The entry explains that its name comes from the title given to works placed after Aristotle’s writings on nature, not from a simple idea that the subject is “beyond physics.” Earlier philosophers often linked metaphysics with being itself, first causes, and unchanging things. Later philosophers widened the field to include topics once treated as physics or other branches of philosophy. Important questions concern categories of being, universals, and substances. A universal would be a shared property or relation, while a substance would exist in its own right. Contemporary metaphysics also studies possibility and necessity, space and time, how objects persist, whether one object can constitute another, causation, determinism and free will, the mental and physical, and social entities. Philosophers disagree about the right method and even about whether metaphysics is a possible discipline.
key_ideas: The meaning of metaphysics has changed. It once centered more narrowly on unchanging reality and first causes, but it now covers many philosophical problems.
Questions about categories ask whether reality contains basic kinds of things, and questions about universals ask whether shared features are real.
Substance theories ask what exists in its own right and how an object can remain the same while changing.
Newer metaphysical questions include whether possibilities belong to things, whether time really passes, and how causes, minds, bodies, and social groups fit into reality.
Philosophers use different approaches: some emphasize science, some what a theory must say exists, and some what is most basic or explains other facts.
Some thinkers argue that metaphysics is impossible because its statements are meaningless or because humans cannot know their answers.
summaries.why_it_matters: Metaphysics examines ideas that appear in everyday thinking but are easy to take for granted. It asks whether objects, properties, causes, possibilities, minds, and social groups have the kinds of reality we assume. These questions connect philosophy with science, logic, ethics, and social life, and they help us understand what a philosophical explanation is supposed to accomplish.

important_terms.definition: A branch of philosophy that investigates the most general questions about reality and what kinds of things exist.
The study of being or existence, especially questions about what it means for something to be real.
A feature or relation that can be shared by many particular things, such as whiteness or being taller than something.
A thing thought to exist independently, rather than existing only as a feature of another thing.
Ideas about what could happen, what must happen, and what could not happen.
A complete way the world could have been, used to discuss possibility and necessity.
The relation between a thing and its parts, or between facts about a whole and facts about its parts.
The view that universals are real in some sense; nominalism is the opposing view that universals do not exist in that way.

questions_to_think_about: If two objects share every part and place, must they be the same object?
Is a property such as redness something real, or only a way of grouping particular red things?
Does the future already exist in the same way as the present, or is the present special?
If choices are caused by earlier events, does that rule out freedom? If choices are partly chance, does that make them free?
Can a school, sports team, or currency be a real thing even though it depends on people and social practices?
